name: Mar Paharia of Dumka
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Dasgupta, Dipankar. 1978. A Descriptive Study of Mal-Pahariya. (grammar sketch per Glottolog; not online)

new_statements.quote: Each Malpaharia word is uttered with a stress on the initial syllable which is not phonemic but a mere breath group only e.g. /muˡĩ/, /turũˡthe/, /kiˡsrOkOme/, /sãˡpTOk/, /khOˡtOm keˡra huibek/, /taˡhar upae/, /huˡdis keˡrĩchO/ 'I have found out the way quickly how the shake will called?'
new_statements.citation: Mukherjee, Kakali. 2023. Malpaharia. In Language Division, Office of the Registrar General, India, Linguistic Survey of India — Jharkhand, pp. 869-939. Section 2 Phonology, 'Stress'.
new_statements.locator: printed p. 881 (PDF p. 898), section 2 Phonology, subsection 'Stress' (between 'Oral vs. Nasalized Vowel' and 'Juncture')
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable of every word; it is predictable (non-phonemic) and treated as a breath-group phenomenon rather than a contrastive feature. Intonation (rising question, falling exclamation, level statement) is described separately as distinctive at phrase level.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. (Note: in the printed examples the stress mark ˡ is placed after the first syllable, e.g. /muˡĩ/, /kiˡsrOkOme/, which is consistent with marking the initial syllable as stressed; the running English gloss of the example string is garbled in the original.)
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word ('Each Malpaharia word'), with examples drawn from a running sentence; the author also equates the stress domain with a breath group. Based on one month of field data from Dumka-Godda (Santal Parganas, Jharkhand) in 1988, published 2023.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is from the LSI-Jharkhand chapter "Malpaharia" (fieldwork Dumka-Godda, Santal Parganas, 1988), i.e. the same Dumka Indo-Aryan variety Glottolog's malp1246 is built on (Glottolog names it "Mar Paharia of Dumka" after Dasgupta 1978). Not to be confused with the Dravidian Malto/"Mal Pahariya" varieties Sauria Paharia [mjt] / Kumarbhag Paharia [kmj], which some census and ethnographic sources lump under the same name.
